key_insight: Language models can be taught not just to answer questions, but to decide when to abstain. In this study, a learned answer selector outperformed the original model's direct responses by improving threshold-averaged utility.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of reliable uncertainty handling in factual question answering: how to reduce harmful confident mistakes while preserving correct answers by enabling models to say "I don't know" when appropriate.
method: Evaluate two abstention strategies on Qwen3-14B: (1) training the model to make the answer/abstain decision itself, and (2) training a separate selector to judge whether the model's answer should be accepted.
Use a utility-based score that rewards correct answers, penalizes wrong answers, and permits abstention as a valid option.
Compare performance across three random seeds and two held-out confidence thresholds to test robustness and calibration.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests that post-hoc answer selection or calibration can make large language models safer and more reliable on factual tasks. It offers a practical path to reducing hallucinations without requiring the base model to always answer.

paper_title: Can Language Models Learn When to Abstain? Policy Learning and Calibrated Answer Selection
paper_authors: Juan Terven, Diana-Margarita Córdova-Esparza, Ruben Gomez, Carlos Miranda Rocha, Julio-Alejandro Romero-González
